engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Opening Principle #3: Castle Early
chess.body: King safety is non-negotiable in the opening. Castle within the first 10 moves. An uncastled king in the centre is a target. After castling, your king is protected by 3 pawns and 2 corner squares. Rooks also connect after castling. Rule: castle before you attack.

wisdom.title: Rest is Productive
wisdom.body: High performers rest. Sleep is not laziness — it's when the brain consolidates learning, the body repairs, emotional regulation resets. Cutting sleep to work more is borrowing from tomorrow's performance to pay today's anxiety. Protect 7 hours. It will make you a better analyst, better father, better human.

book.author: James Clear
book.chapter: The 1% Rule: Why Small Gains Compound Into Extraordinary Results
book.lesson: If you get 1% better every day for a year, you end up 37 times better. If you get 1% worse, you decay to nearly zero. Most people overestimate what they can do in a day and underestimate what they can do in a year of consistent 1% improvements. Clear's central insight: you don't rise to the level of your goals, you fall to the level of your systems. Goals are for direction. Systems are for progress.
book.key_quote: Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement.
book.action: Identify one tiny habit you can improve by 1% today. Stack it onto an existing behaviour: after [CURRENT HABIT], I will [NEW HABIT].
crux: You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.
1% better daily compounds to 37x in a year. 1% worse decays to 0.03x.
Habits form on a four-step loop: cue → craving → response → reward.
Build good habits: make it obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying. Invert all four to break one.
Identity drives behaviour, not the reverse. 'I don't smoke' beats 'I'm trying to quit'.
Every action is a vote for the person you are becoming. Majority wins, not unanimity.
The two-minute rule: a new habit must take under two minutes to start.
Environment beats willpower. Motivation is overrated; friction is decisive.
Habit stacking: after [existing habit], I will [new habit]. The old habit becomes the cue.
You need a plateau of latent potential. Results lag effort — most people quit inside the lag.
Never miss twice. One miss is an accident. Two is the start of a new habit.
Measure what you want to repeat. An unrecorded habit drifts within three weeks.
learnings: Discipline is a design problem, not a character problem.
The gap between effort and visible result is where nearly everyone quits.
Systems survive bad days. Motivation does not.
Tracking is not admin. Tracking is the habit.
examples: British Cycling went from one Tour de France win in 110 years to five in six years by stacking 1% gains — pillow hygiene, hand-washing, bike paint for dust visibility.
Clear's own recovery: a bat to the face at 15, two years of rebuilding, then an academic All-American — built entirely on sleep and study routines, not talent.
Twice-weekly gym attendance beats a 90-minute session once a month, even though the monthly total is similar. Frequency builds identity; volume does not.
adapt: Score one caption per day before posting. The score is the habit, not the post.
Two-minute rule on the Dubai job hunt: open the tracker and add one company. That is the whole commitment.
SIP on auto-debit the day salary lands. Remove the monthly decision entirely.
Never miss twice on the daily brief. One skipped morning is fine. Two means the system broke.

minimalism.title: One Screen, One Task
minimalism.body: Seventeen open tabs is not research, it is deferred decisions rendered in pixels. Each one is a small unfinished thought.
minimalism.action: Close every tab. Bookmark what genuinely matters — usually two.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Learn The Name, Use The Name
etiquette.body: Names are the cheapest respect available and the most noticed when withheld. Repeat it immediately on hearing it. Ask the spelling. Ask the pronunciation — getting it wrong twice is careless, asking once is respect.
etiquette.action: Learn one colleague's name properly today. Use it twice.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: Simplify The Morning
stillness.body: Same breakfast. Same order. Same route. Ritual removes decisions from the hours when your judgement is most valuable and least replaceable.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Occam's Razor
model.body: The explanation requiring fewest assumptions is usually right. Elaborate theories feel like insight and are mostly the mind pattern-matching on noise.
model.action: Take your most complex current explanation. Find the simpler one.
model.label: Mental Model

arabic.use: The standard farewell. Said to the person leaving.

drill.title: Read A Cash Flow Statement First
drill.body: Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. Most analysts start at revenue. Start at operating cash flow and compare it to net income — the gap is where the story is.
drill.action: Pull one company's cash flow. Find the largest gap to net income. Explain it.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Fibre, Not Supplements
health.body: Most people get under half the recommended 30g. Fibre feeds the gut microbiome, blunts glucose response, and is one of the few dietary factors with consistent large-cohort support.
health.action: Add one high-fibre food today. Legumes, oats, or berries.
health.label: Health

quote.name: Andrew Carnegie
quote.quote: Anything in life worth having is worth working for.

lesson.lesson: We must all suffer one of two things: the pain of discipline or the pain of regret.

case.title: Infosys: The Global Delivery Model
case.story: Narayana Murthy started Infosys with ₹10,000 borrowed from his wife in 1981. Built the global delivery model — offshore talent, onshore management. Revenue: $18B+.
case.lesson: Arbitrage is a legitimate business model. Take a global problem, apply local economics, execute flawlessly. Consistency beats creativity in services.

fpna.title: Free Cash Flow
fpna.body: FCF = Net Income + D&A – Capex – ΔNWC. A company can show profit and still run out of cash.

cfo.title: FC Step 1: Own the Close
cfo.body: Financial Controllers close the books — every month, clean, on time, no surprises. Speed + accuracy is the baseline. If close takes 10 days, get it to 5. Automate reconciliations. Build a close checklist and hit it every time.

money_hack.title: EPF Power
money_hack.body: EPF gives 8.25% guaranteed, tax-free. Max out VPF if your employer allows.

dubai.title: Attestation is the silent blocker
dubai.body: Degree and CA certificate need MEA attestation in India, then UAE embassy attestation, then MOFA in the UAE. Three to six weeks if nothing goes wrong. Offers have been withdrawn over this.
dubai.targets: Start it before you have an offer. It expires slowly and costs little.
dubai.action: Roughly ₹8–15K all-in per document, and the only thing it buys is not losing the job.

desk.productivity: Weekly financial review: 10 min. Net worth, cash flow, investments.

father.title: Wait out the frustration noise
father.do: When she grumbles at a task, wait. Only step in if it escalates to genuine distress.
father.why: There is a difference between frustration and distress, and learning to tell them apart is a skill you build now. Frustration tolerated becomes persistence; frustration always rescued becomes helplessness.

father.title: Check the floor at her eye level
father.do: Lie on the floor and look across the room from her height. Remove what you find.
father.why: Mobility arrives suddenly. Anything reachable at that height will be in her mouth within days of her crawling, and you will not get advance notice.

life_wisdom.teaching: Jain metaphysics treats karma as fine matter that adheres to the soul through action and intent. Unusually, intent matters as much as the act.
life_wisdom.apply: Judge your own decisions on intent and process, not only outcome. A profitable trade taken for bad reasons still deposits the bad habit.

life_wisdom.teaching: The doctrine that there is no fixed, unchanging self — what feels like a permanent 'I' is a process, continually reconstructed.
life_wisdom.apply: When you catch yourself saying 'I am not a numbers-under-pressure person', notice that is a description of a habit, not a fact about you.

speaking.title: Breathe before the hard part
speaking.drill: Identify the toughest sentence in an answer and take a full breath immediately before it.
speaking.why: Nerves shorten breath, which raises pitch and speeds delivery precisely when you most need authority.

interview_tech.q: Walk me through how a $1M inventory write-down flows through all three statements.
interview_tech.a: P&L: COGS up $1M, so gross profit, EBIT and pre-tax income each fall $1M. At a 25% rate, net income falls $750K. Cash flow: start from net income −$750K, add back the $1M non-cash write-down, so operating cash flow rises $250K — the tax shield. Balance sheet: inventory −$1M, cash +$250K, so assets fall $750K; retained earnings fall $750K. It balances. The point they are testing: you know the write-down is non-cash and that the only real cash effect is tax.

interview_tech.q: How do you value a new store before signing a 10-year lease?
interview_tech.a: Build an unlevered free cash flow model over the lease term. Revenue from catchment population, comparable sales density and a ramp curve — never assume year-one maturity. Deduct COGS, rent with escalation clauses, staff, and allocated overhead only if genuinely incremental. Capex is fit-out plus initial inventory. Discount at WACC and test IRR versus hurdle, payback, and NPV. Then sensitise the two variables that actually decide it: year-one sales and the ramp. A store that only clears the hurdle at 100% of forecast is a no.

interview_soft.q: How do you stay current technically while managing?
interview_soft.a: Be specific and verifiable. Name the standard you last read in full and why, the technical update you attended, the thing you built yourself recently rather than delegated. Vague answers about 'reading widely' land badly with technical interviewers. The strongest version connects it to a decision: 'I went back through IFRS 16 properly when we hit the lease modification question on the Indonesian stores, and that changed how we structured the renewal.'

interview_soft.q: Where do you think retail is heading in the next five years?
interview_soft.a: Have a view and defend it with numbers, not trends. Something like: physical stores stop being judged on their own sales as fulfilment and returns blur the channels, which breaks conventional store P&L and forces a catchment-level view; margin pressure shifts from price to cost-to-serve; and in the Gulf specifically, corporate tax and e-invoicing professionalise finance functions that were previously light. Then say what you would do about it in the role you are interviewing for.
